message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the key protections and responsibilities that apply to residential tenants in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and general landlord‑tenant law. For specific situations—especially those involving disputes, evictions, or lease negotiations—consult a qualified attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written move‑in inspection log.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Report problems in writing (email or certified mail).
• If the landlord fails to fix, you may withhold rent (after giving notice) or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct claim. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease; late fees are limited to **$25** per day for a single late payment, or **$50** for a second late payment. | • Keep receipts or bank records. | | **Lease Terms** | • The lease must be in writing for **any term longer than one year**.
• The lease cannot contain any **unreasonable or illegal** clauses (e.g., waiving your right to a habitable dwelling). | • Review the lease carefully before signing; ask for clarification on any ambiguous terms. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord may not enter the premises without **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours) except in emergencies. | • Document any unauthorized entries; you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office or local housing agency. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on **race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income** (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must provide a **written notice** (30 days for nonpayment, 60 days for lease violations, 90 days for no‑cause termination of a month‑to‑month lease).
• Eviction must be pursued through the court; landlords cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond promptly to notices; negotiate or seek mediation if possible. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a habitability issue within a reasonable time after notice, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent (up to the amount of the rent). | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has **no statewide rent‑control laws**. | • Be aware that rent increases are generally at the landlord’s discretion, subject to lease terms. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Lease may restrict subletting; if allowed, you must obtain written permission. | • Obtain written consent before subletting; keep copies. | | **Insurance** | • Landlord is not required to carry insurance for your personal property. | • Consider renter’s insurance to protect your belongings. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for breach of contract, damages, or unlawful eviction. | • Small claims court can handle disputes up to $20,000. | | **Local Ordinances** | • Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas, Houston) have additional tenant protections, such as rent‑increase caps or eviction moratoria. | • Check your city’s housing department website for local rules. | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read the Lease** – Verify rent amount, security deposit limits, pet policies, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and inspection reports. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – Understand how much notice you need to give before moving out or how much notice the landlord must give you. 4. **Report Issues Promptly** – Write a formal notice for repairs; give the landlord a reasonable window to respond. 5. **Keep Records of Payments** – Use online banking or written receipts to prove timely rent payments. 6. **Seek Mediation** – Many cities offer free or low‑cost mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. 7. **Know Your Local Laws** – Check your city or county’s housing regulations for additional protections. --- #### When to Seek Legal Help - **Unlawful Eviction**: If you’re being forced out without proper notice or court order. - **Discrimination Claims**: If you suspect the landlord is violating fair‑housing laws. - **Major Habitability Issues**: If the landlord refuses to fix serious problems (e.g., mold, broken heating). - **Large Security Deposit Disputes**: If the landlord withholds more than the statutory amount or fails to provide an itemized statement. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Consumer complaints, tenant‑rights guides | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Discrimination complaints | https://www.tchra.org | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Fair housing information, filing complaints | https://www.hud.gov | | **Local Housing Agencies** | City‑specific tenant‑rights information, mediation services | Search “[Your City] housing agency” | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Filing civil claims up to $20,000 | https://www.txcourts.gov/small-claims/ | | **Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Legal clinics, advocacy | Search “tenant rights Texas” | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, a clear lease, reasonable notice before entry or eviction, and protection against discrimination. Keep thorough records, communicate in writing, and know the local ordinances that may add extra safeguards. If you encounter a problem that you can’t resolve on your own, reach out to a tenant‑rights group or attorney for guidance.
